# Sidelit roadmap

## Batch review notes

Status: implemented in v0.4.0. One local list, 20 notes, and one immutable batch delivery record. Add to review is the explicit local-save action. No task history, automatic sending, or completion tracking.

While reading, collect several selected passages or elements with individual
Explain, Review, or Edit instructions. Keep reading without sending each note
immediately, then review the collection and send it deliberately to an existing
Pi session. Keep the interface compact; this is a review list, not agent chat.

Acceptance criteria:

- Add a note from text selection, element inspection, or the current document.
  Each note retains its instruction, intent, document identity and capture version.
- Keep saved notes when hiding the composer, changing tabs, refreshing, or exiting.
  Composer edits require Add to review, Save note, or Save to Notes on exit before
  they are stored. Quit, window close, and update/restart offer Save to Notes /
  Discard / Cancel for unsent requests and unsaved note edits; failed saves stop exit.
- Show a concise list with edit, remove and Reveal selection actions. Reattachment
  must fail closed, and stale or unsaved context must remain visible.
- Let the user choose which notes to send, inspect the final payload and explicitly
  select the target. Never silently combine different projects or change intent.
- Bound both individual notes and the aggregate message. Freeze sent IDs, payloads
  and destination; safely retry uncertain delivery without duplicating accepted notes.
- Distinguish unsent, received and accepted notes. Busy or disconnected Pi sessions
  must not lose notes or misrepresent delivery as completed work. Answers stay in Pi.
- Test multiple documents, stale captures, partial failures, retries, keyboard use,
  and the minimum window size. Preserve the single-request path and editor safety.

Current behavior and delivery semantics are documented in [README.md](README.md).

## Send to any agent

Status: Copy as prompt shipped in 0.9.0; direct delivery not started. Today requests only reach Pi directly. Let them reach Claude Code,
Codex, and other agents in sessions that are already running.

Likely approach, from reading how [Orca](https://github.com/stablyai/orca) does it:

- Keep the Pi bridge, which has the strongest receipts.
- For agents in Rex panes, paste the request and press Enter with
  `com.superlogical.terminal.write`, then watch `com.superlogical.terminal.program_status`
  for a turn starting. No start flags or restart should be needed.
- For everything else, add Copy as prompt.

To decide first: this reverses the rule that delivery never types into a terminal.

Requirements if it goes ahead:

- Never send to a pane that is waiting on permission, or whose process has changed.
  Enter could answer the dialog.
- Don't submit text the person has half typed. Orca doesn't appear to guard against this;
  reading the screen first needs a parser for each agent.
- Say what was actually confirmed. Sidelit can show "sent" and "a turn started" but can't
  tie a turn to a request, and an already busy agent gives no confirmation at all.
- Carry the no-edit instruction for Explain and Review through every route.
- Discovery only accepts a process named `pi`; Claude's process name is its version, so
  match on `argv0` or the status app.

Unverified: `write` hasn't been tried. `program_status` has only been seen on one Claude
Code pane; Orca's matrix lists Codex and Pi as reporting it too. Paste timing differs by
agent, so check Orca's `src/shared/agent-prompt-injection.ts` (MIT) first. Fallbacks if
typing is ruled out: Claude Code channels (research preview, needs a start flag) and the
Codex app server or `codex queue`.

# Product

<!-- impeccable:product-schema 1 -->

## Platform
web

Desktop UI in Tauri's OS webview. macOS first; portable to Linux.

## Stack
Tauri 2 and Rust; React, TypeScript, Vite, Crepe, and lazy-loaded Monaco. No Electron or Node runtime.

## Users and purpose
Developers use Rex for terminals, Pi for agent work, and Neovim for general source editing. Sidelit renders Markdown, HTML, and MDX, captures bounded text/element context, and sends an Explain, Review, or Edit request to an existing Pi session. The core loop is read → select or inspect → request → follow up in Pi → refresh. It is not an IDE, terminal emulator, or chat harness.

## Constraints
Files are the source of truth. Explicit saves, safe conflict handling, offline local previews, native dialogs, and one application instance. Preserve Crepe and Monaco; isolate executable previews. Pi delivery is local-only, acknowledged, and uses its native follow-up queue, never terminal typing. No cloud, agent chat, server process manager, or proprietary storage.

Sidelit keeps one quick-request draft in memory; hiding it and switching tabs preserve it, but app exit does not. After Send, a new selection action starts a fresh request. The Requests sidebar shows up to 100 recent quick requests for the current document during this app session. Earlier requests keep their receipts, frozen retry payloads, and change reports; pending or uncertain deliveries are never evicted to make room. History is not saved across restarts. Add to review explicitly saves a note locally. One bounded list holds up to 20 notes across restarts, separate from document recovery. Selected notes from one project or live-page origin can be sent as one batch to an explicitly chosen Pi session. One batch delivery attempt is retained until the user removes it; there is no task history or automatic sending. Sidelit shows when Pi finishes its turn, which never means the request succeeded. Captured context remains tied to its original document and version: unsaved captures are labelled, changed file context needs explicit acknowledgment, and replacing an unsent draft's selection requires explicit consent. A delivery attempt is immutable, including retries. Answers belong in Pi; delivery, acceptance, or a finished turn is not completion.

## Brand commitments
Sidelit is a working name. The user requested Rex's native structure: blue-charcoal surfaces, quiet icons and soft tabs, without copying its terminal layout. The Fold icon now supplies amber and burnt-orange action accents. Minimal chrome, compact controls, subtle borders, clear focus, and maximum preview space. New installs use Dark; preserve explicit System or Light preferences. Rendered text uses IBM Plex Sans; monospace uses Inconsolata. HTML and dev servers retain their own page styles.

## Decisions
The brief supplies the product and visual direction; no extra interview is needed. Rendered Markdown defaults to reading, with explicit Edit for local changes and Source when needed. Selection-adjacent Explain and Review ask Pi to answer without editing files; request Edit requires a change instruction. A compact contextual composer can be hidden and reopened; a persistent attachment highlight and Reveal selection reconnect it to the document only when the capture can be located safely. Show in Rex returns to a linked Pi session. Never choose an ambiguous agent target or label a bridge receipt as completed work. Retain appearance preferences without remounting editors.

Approved additions: New File and Save As with native, no-clobber creation; workspace Quick Open; editable conflict comparison; review of the latest clean external change; frontmatter-preserving rendered editing; and opt-in local session recovery. Recovery stays separate from the original Markdown, requires fresh native folder approval, keeps only the latest checkpoint for seven days, and provides an off-and-delete control. Later approved: changes marked against the last reviewed version or the last commit, per-passage revert into the draft, optional attachment of unsaved changes to a request, a finished-turn status, agent pointers with `--find`, an outline with heading anchors, read-only Git status, math drawn while reading, saved review marks, a list of documents that changed during a request, agent walkthroughs, and Find in the rich editor. No version-history system, cloud service, or embedded agent runtime was added. Public GitHub releases supply signed app updates: check on startup and daily, install and restart only after user approval and safe draft handling. Document text and paths are not sent in update requests.

With 0.9.0 out, here's what I'd do next, in rough priority order.

## 1. Fix what's already on the roadmap
- **Ghost scroll bug.** This is the only open item that's actually a bug, and it hits the core loop of reading and selecting. Start with a repro: does it happen on first open, after a disk reload, or after a mode switch? Then check whether the initial scroll position is applied twice, and whether a Crepe redraw (math decorations, change marks) moves the view.
- **Sidebar icons and tooltips.** The "modified" and "marked reviewed" icons look too alike, and some icons have no tooltip. Both are small fixes that would make the app noticeably clearer. I'd ship them together as a 0.9.1.

## 2. Add tests where the risk is
- **`updates.rs` has no Rust tests**, even though invariant 13 (signed, version-matched, no silent install) is one of the strictest rules in the project. `updater-smoke.py` covers the full flow, but unit tests for refusing unsigned or mismatched updates would catch problems much sooner.
- `cli.rs` and `preview.rs` have one test each. `cli.rs` handles the queued handoff and `--find` pointers, and both are easy to break quietly.
- These frontend files have no tests: `QuickOpen.tsx`, `ToolDialogs.tsx` (Check Links and Compare with Commit, both new in 0.9.0), `RequestChanges.tsx`, and `SessionDialog.tsx`. The last two carry invariant 16's "finished isn't success" wording, so a small render test should check that the wording stays.

## 3. Split up `App.tsx`
At 1,586 lines with about 54 `useState` calls, it's the main obstacle to adding features. I'd move the workspace/tree, the dialog state and the keyboard actions into hooks or modules, the same way `closing.ts` and `recovery.ts` were split out. A refactor like this is worth doing before the next big feature, not after.

## 4. Decide on "Send to any agent"
This is the biggest product question left. Copy as prompt shipped, but direct delivery would break the rule that delivery never types into a terminal. Before writing any code I'd test the two unverified pieces first: does `terminal.write` work, and does `program_status` report correctly for Claude Code and Codex panes? If either fails, Claude Code channels or `codex queue` avoid the terminal problem completely.

## 5. Drop the "real browser renderer" idea for now
The sandboxed opaque-origin iframe is what invariant 6 depends on. A real browser engine would make that much harder to keep, and nothing so far suggests WKWebView is too limited. I'd remove it from the roadmap unless a specific HTML/MDX document renders wrong.

## Smaller ideas
- Search in Files and Check Links are both new. Running them on a large repo would show whether their limits feel right in practice.
- Linux is listed as "portable" in PRODUCT.md, but the desktop smoke test only checks packaged WKWebView on macOS. A Linux (WebKitGTK) check would back up that claim.

If you want somewhere to start, I'd take the ghost scroll repro plus the icon fixes as a quick 0.9.1, then the `updates.rs` tests.

content.text:
I've made the three fixes and updated the roadmap. Nothing is committed yet.

## Ghost scroll
I found two likely causes and fixed both:
- **Old reveals replayed on remount.** After you use Reveal selection once, the rich editor and HTML preview scrolled back to that selection every time they remounted (tab switch, Source→Rendered). Each one tracked the last reveal in a ref that reset to 0. Reveals are now claimed once across the app, the same way jumps already were (`src/jump.ts`, used in `Rich.tsx` and `Preview.tsx`). New test: `tests/jump.test.ts`.
- **Images collapsing.** Images arrive with no size, so whenever an image view is recreated (for example a disk reload after an agent edit), images above the viewport shrink to 0 and then grow back. WebKit doesn't compensate for that, so the page jumps. The editor now remembers each image's last size and reserves that space.

I couldn't reproduce the bug here, so this still needs checking on the Mac. If it still drifts, the next suspect is Mermaid and math drawing after the scroll position has been restored.

## Sidebar icons
The folder "contains changes" Git mark was the same filled accent dot as a tab's unsaved-changes dot. It's now a hollow ring. The unsaved dot now has a tooltip, and the Git tooltips start with "Git:". I couldn't find any sidebar mark for "marked reviewed". If you meant a different icon, point me at it.

## `updates.rs` tests
I moved the version check and the insecure-transport check into small functions and added 3 tests, including one that checks the shipped `tauri.conf.json` has a public key, HTTPS-only endpoints, and none of the "dangerous" flags.

## Checks
- `pnpm check` and `pnpm test` pass (264 tests).
- `cargo fmt --check` is clean.
- `cargo test` **can't build on arthur**: the GTK/WebKit dev libraries aren't installed. I compiled and ran the new updater tests in a standalone crate instead, and all 3 pass. The full Rust suite still needs a run on the Mac.

## Send to any agent on zaphod
I'd develop it on zaphod. Arthur can't build the app at all, the desktop smoke test only covers macOS, and the investigation needs real Claude Code, Codex and Pi sessions in Rex panes. Rex has no hosts set up here, so either start a session on zaphod or add it with `rex hosts add zaphod <endpoint>` and I can drive it from here. The first step is still the one in the roadmap: confirm that `terminal.write` and `program_status` work for each agent before writing any delivery code.

I also removed the "real browser renderer" entry from ROADMAP.md. Want me to commit this as the start of 0.9.1?

result.output:
# Release Sidelit

Users install the DMG from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/heath0xFF/sidelit/releases/latest). The repository and downloads are public. Users do not need build tools or a GitHub account.

## Publish a version

1. Set the same `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` version in `package.json`, `src-tauri/Cargo.toml`, and `src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`. Each release needs a new version.
2. Run `cargo check --manifest-path src-tauri/Cargo.toml` to update the package version in `src-tauri/Cargo.lock`. Keep both lockfiles committed.
3. Update the release notes in `.github/workflows/release.yml`, run the checks, then commit and push to `main`.
4. Open **Actions → Release macOS → Run workflow**, select **main**, and run it. A pushed matching version tag also starts the workflow.
5. Wait for the job to pass. It uploads all assets to a draft release, then publishes it as the latest release.

The tag must match the committed app version. An existing tag must point to the build's exact commit. Published versions and assets are not overwritten. If an upload fails and leaves a draft, remove only that failed draft before retrying from the same tag.

## Build and release checks

The macOS workflow:

- Uses pinned actions, the configured pnpm version, Node 24, stable Rust, and committed lockfiles.
- Runs type checks, frontend and Rust tests, and Rust formatting.
- Rejects desktop-test runtime dependencies, insecure updater settings, and downgrade settings.
- Builds a universal Apple Silicon + Intel `.app` and `.dmg`, without `desktop-test`.
- Creates and signs `Sidelit.app.tar.gz` with the version in its trusted signature comment.
- Checks both architectures, the app signature, the DMG, and its Applications shortcut.
- Runs `src-tauri/examples/update-manifest.rs` to verify the archive with the public update key and confirm its signed version before writing `latest.json`.
- Publishes the DMG, update archive, `.sig`, `latest.json`, and `SHA256SUMS.txt`. Both Mac architectures use the same universal archive.

GitHub supplies the release token. No personal token is required. Protect changes to the release workflow: a workflow that can access the signing secret can sign app updates.

These checks do not replace packaged desktop smoke tests or native-dialog checks in `VERIFICATION.md`. Intel is cross-built, not run on Intel hardware here. Windows and Linux installers are not published.

## Update signing key

The committed public key is in `src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`. The private key is the GitHub Actions secret **`TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY`**. The current key has no passphrase; the workflow supplies an empty signing password.

The maintainer's local copy is `~/.config/sidelit/release-signing/updater.key`, in a private directory with mode 0600 on the key. It is not stored in Git. **Keep an encrypted backup outside this computer.** GitHub does not let you retrieve a secret's value. Losing this key prevents updates for clients that trust its public key; those users would need a new manual installer.

Do not generate a replacement key for each release. Do not sign test builds with the release key. `scripts/updater-smoke.py` creates a separate disposable key for its isolated app.

The updater requires a signed version and accepts only newer versions. A modified manifest cannot pair an old signed archive with a false new version number. Checks and downloads require HTTPS in ordinary builds. The local updater test explicitly permits HTTP only in its separate test bundle.

## In-app update behavior

Version 0.1.0 has no updater. Users must install 0.1.1 or later from a DMG once.

New clients check the public `releases/latest/download/latest.json` feed on startup and daily while open. Background failures do not interrupt editing. Users can check through Actions or the native Sidelit menu.

Install & Restart uses the same live Save/Discard/Cancel checks as Quit. The app locks editing, flushes enabled recovery, then downloads and verifies the archive before replacement. A failed operation unlocks the editor and keeps drafts. The restart does not reuse a stale CLI file path or handoff receipt. Recovery remains opt-in; without it, the restarted app does not restore tabs.

## Apple signing and notarization

Update signatures and Apple code signatures are separate. Current apps use an **ad-hoc Apple signature** (`signingIdentity: "-"`), not a Developer ID signature or notarization. Browser downloads can still be blocked by Gatekeeper. Use the per-app **Privacy & Security → Open Anyway** control only for a trusted download. Do not disable Gatekeeper system-wide.

For normal first-launch approval, configure a **Developer ID Application** certificate and notarization credentials using [Tauri's macOS signing guide](https://v2.tauri.app/distribute/sign/macos/). An Apple Development certificate is not a substitute. Store credentials in Actions secrets, never Git.

## Local builds and tests

Ordinary local builds do not create update archives, so they do not need a private signing key:

```sh
CI=true pnpm tauri build --ci --bundles app,dmg -- --locked
```

The release workflow explicitly enables `bundle.createUpdaterArtifacts`. To reproduce a signed universal release locally, use the protected key, never a test key:

```sh
rustup target add aarch64-apple-darwin x86_64-apple-darwin
TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY="REDACTED" \
TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD='' CI=true \
pnpm tauri build --ci --target universal-apple-darwin --bundles app,dmg \
  --config '{"bundle":{"createUpdaterArtifacts":true}}' -- --locked
cargo run --manifest-path src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked --example update-manifest -- \
  src-tauri/target/universal-apple-darwin/release/bundle
```

The real install/restart check is `python3 scripts/updater-smoke.py`. It builds only its own `Sidelit Update Check.app`, uses a temporary local feed, and removes the test bundle when finished. Do not put real work in that window. Native administrator approval and browser quarantine still need manual checks.

content.text:
v0.9.1 is committed and tagged (`09818c4`), and both are pushed. The release workflow is still running; the last one took about 9 minutes. It runs the full Rust test suite on macOS before it publishes anything, which covers the `cargo test` I couldn't run here. I'll tell you when it finishes.

## Why arthur can't build
Arthur (Ubuntu 26.04) has a compiler toolchain but none of the Linux libraries Tauri builds against: GTK 3, WebKitGTK 4.1, libsoup 3, librsvg, OpenSSL and the app-indicator library. The Rust build fails on the first of them, in `glib-sys`, before any Sidelit code compiles. The setup docs only covered macOS in detail and linked to Tauri's prerequisites page for Linux, so these were never installed.

Installing them needs sudo, so run this yourself:

```
! sudo apt install libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev libgtk-3-dev libsoup-3.0-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev libssl-dev libxdo-dev build-essential curl wget file
```

After that, I'll run `cargo check` and `cargo test` here, then try `pnpm desktop` to see whether the app runs on Linux. The docs say Linux builds have never been verified.

I've added the same command to the Linux section of `docs/development.md`. It's uncommitted until we've confirmed the package list builds the app on arthur.

Even with arthur building, the **send to any agent** work should still happen on zaphod. That depends on testing real agent sessions in Rex panes and the macOS WebKit view, not just on compiling.
